metaDescription: Six built-in microwaves compared on cutout size, trim kits, sensor cooking and drawer versus wall-oven installs, with fit warnings first.
expertTake: The Frigidaire Gallery GMBS3068BF is the best built-in pick because its 2.2 cubic foot cavity and sensor cooking suit a full-size kitchen remodel. The Frigidaire FMBS2227BB is the value choice for a standard wall cutout. Anyone without a prepared cutout should skip built-ins and buy a countertop oven with a trim kit.
introParagraphs: A built-in microwave sits flush with cabinetry, usually above a wall oven or in a tall cabinet bank. It frees counter space and gives a clean look, but it also locks you into a cutout, a trim kit and a vent path that must be planned before purchase.

Fit is the main decision. Cutout dimensions, trim kit sizes, venting and cabinet depth matter more than cooking features, so this guide starts from those constraints and then compares power, sensors and controls across the lineup.

products.name: Frigidaire Gallery GMBS3068BF 2.2 cu ft built-in microwave
products.description:
Frigidaire Gallery builds this around a very large 2.2 cubic foot cavity, enough for big casserole dishes and several containers at once. Sensors inside the cabinet read the food and set power and time automatically, which keeps reheats from drying out. The trim kit is a separate purchase, and the listing names 27 inch and 30 inch kits, so the cutout decides which one you need.

The cabinet is a true built-in, so plan the electrical outlet, the ventilation and the support shelf before ordering. Compared with the FMBS2227BB, you gain about six tenths of a cubic foot and a Gallery finish. The larger body also demands a deeper cabinet, so check the depth listed on the spec sheet against your wall.

Ownership is quiet if installed correctly. Run a damp cloth through the interior after steamy foods so the sensor reads accurately, and keep the vent path clear. Because the unit is recessed, replacement later means matching the same cutout, which is another reason to buy the right size the first time. For a full kitchen remodel it is the safest pick.
products.bestFor: Remodels that need a large, flush microwave with sensor cooking.
pros: Very large 2.2 cu ft cavity
Sensor cook adjusts power and time
Trim kits available in 27 and 30 in
Flush look frees counter space
cons: Trim kit is an extra purchase
Replacing later requires the same cutout size

products.name: Frigidaire PMBS3080BF 2.2 cu ft built-in sensor microwave
products.description:
This Frigidaire Professional model also offers 2.2 cubic feet and sensor cook, but the sheet is more explicit about size. The body is about 24 3/8 inches wide, 19 5/8 inches deep and 13 5/8 inches tall, with a cutout of roughly 24 3/4 inches wide and 20 inches deep. A 30 inch trim kit is required and sold separately, so it is built for a standard 30 inch cabinet opening.

The practical difference from the Gallery is the clear published dimensions. For installers, those numbers matter because a built-in that is a half inch too wide cannot be forced. Sensor cooking reads moisture so that power and time adjust for the food.

Care is routine: wipe the interior, check the vent and leave the trim kit alone once installed. It is the right pick when your cabinet opening already matches a 30 inch kit and you want the same cavity size as the Gallery without paying for Gallery styling.
products.bestFor: Installers working to a published 30 inch cabinet cutout.
pros: Published body and cutout dimensions
2.2 cu ft cavity for large dishes
Sensor cook adjusts power and time
30 in trim kit fits a standard opening
cons: Trim kit required and sold separately
Deep cabinet needed at about 20 in
Wide body leaves little shelf margin

products.name: Frigidaire FMBS2227BB 1.6 cu ft built-in microwave, black
products.description:
The FMBS2227BB is the smaller, lower-cost way to get a built-in. A 1.6 cubic foot cavity handles dinner plates and medium casserole dishes, and both sensor cook and sensor reheat adjust power and time for common foods. The black finish blends with dark cabinetry or black appliance suites.

Trim kits are sold separately in 27 inch and 30 inch sizes, so pick one that matches the cutout. A smaller cabinet also eases the depth requirement compared with the 2.2 cubic foot models. Sensor reheat is the useful extra, since it brings leftovers up to temperature without guesswork.

Take a cloth to the interior after use and keep the vent path clear. For a kitchen with a standard cutout and no need for a huge cavity, this is the economical choice.
products.bestFor: Standard remodels that want sensor cooking in a smaller built-in.
pros: Sensor cook and sensor reheat
Black finish suits dark cabinetry
Smaller body eases cabinet depth
Trim kits for 27 and 30 in cutouts
cons: 1.6 cu ft is smaller than the Gallery

products.name: Summit SMBI24 24 in built-in microwave with trim kit
products.description:
Summit sells this 24 inch built-in with the trim kit included, which is rare in this lineup. The cabinet opening is about 15 3/4 inches high, 22 1/2 inches wide and 18 1/4 inches deep, so it fits shorter, tighter spaces than the Frigidaire models. A front-venting design lets you place it above or below a counter or over a wall oven.

Output is 1000 watts with multiple power levels and presets for popcorn, pizza and beverages by weight or time. It has no listed sensor, so you set the cooking yourself. Next to the Frigidaire FMBS2227BB, you save the trim kit cost and the sensor features.

Front venting means heat leaves through the front, so keep that area clear. It suits a compact kitchen or an island where a full 30 inch cutout is not available.
products.bestFor: Compact or island installs that need a smaller 24 in cutout.
pros: Trim kit included in the package
Front venting allows flexible placement
Smaller 22.5 in wide cutout
Weight or time presets
cons: 1000 W output with a smaller cavity

products.name: AAOBOSI 24 in 1.6 cu ft built-in microwave convection air fryer combo
products.description:
AAOBOSI folds convection and an air fryer mode into a 24 inch built-in microwave, so one cabinet can heat, brown and crisp. Ten power levels sit alongside functions such as auto defrost, soften and melt, and sensor options, and a glass touchpad drives six auto menus.

The combo approach saves space in a small kitchen that cannot fit a separate wall oven. It also means more parts to maintain, since convection elements and fans age differently from a magnetron. The brand has less service reach than Frigidaire, so check warranty and support before buying.

Give the interior a wipe after browning functions, since grease bakes on faster than in a plain microwave. Choose it for someone who wants a single built-in that replaces both a microwave and a small oven.
products.bestFor: Small kitchens that want microwave, convection and air frying in one built-in.
pros: Convection and air fryer functions
Glass touchpad with six auto menus
Ten functions including soften and sensor
24 in width fits compact cabinets
cons: More parts to wear than a plain microwave
Grease bakes on faster after browning

products.name: Sharp SMD2420MS 24 in built-in microwave drawer 1.2 cu ft
products.description:
Sharp's drawer pulls out instead of swinging a door, so you slide dishes in at waist height rather than lifting them over a counter edge. The interior is roughly 17 by 16 inches with 1.2 cubic feet of capacity, big enough for platters, and Sensor Cook detects moisture to set time automatically.

It can be installed in a wall, island, peninsula or under a counter, which gives more flexibility than a classic over-range cut. The touch control panel stays clean, and accessibility is the big draw for people who cannot lift hot food high.

A drawer unit costs more and needs careful cabinet planning. Keep the guide rails clear of spills, and wipe the interior after use. Best suited to accessible kitchens and islands.
products.bestFor: Accessible kitchens and islands where lifting hot dishes is a concern.
pros: Pull-out drawer opens at waist height
Wide 17 x 16 in interior fits platters
Sensor Cook sets time by moisture
Installs under counter or in an island
cons: Costs more than a door-style built-in

buyingCriteria.explanation: A built-in is chosen by the hole it fills. The Frigidaire PMBS3080BF lists a cutout of about 24 3/4 inches wide and 20 inches deep, while the Summit SMBI24 opens about 22 1/2 inches wide and 18 1/4 inches deep. Trim kits for the Frigidaire units are sold separately in 27 inch and 30 inch versions. Measure the cabinet, not the old microwave, because a half inch too narrow cannot be fixed afterward. Also confirm that the cabinet floor can carry the weight and that a grounded outlet sits inside or beside the opening. Many remodels fail at this step, when an installer finds the outlet blocked by the new body.

The Gallery GMBS3068BF reaches 2.2 cubic feet, and the FMBS2227BB is 1.6 cubic feet. Bigger cavities need deeper cabinets, so confirm the depth from the sheet. A 2.2 cubic foot cavity is useful for platters, while a 1.6 cubic foot unit handles dinner plates with less cabinet work. Most households rarely need the biggest cavity, so do not pay for volume that you will not fill. Turntable width and door opening are the better practical measures of what fits.

Built-ins vent through the front or the back, and the Summit SMBI24 vents to the front so it can sit above a wall oven. A microwave jammed against a wall will overheat its magnetron. Follow the clearances in the installation manual, and never block vents with a shelf or appliance above.

The Frigidaire Gallery, PMBS3080BF and FMBS2227BB all list sensor cook, and the FMBS2227BB adds sensor reheat. The Summit relies on weight or time presets. Sensors help when the food varies, but covered dishes can fool them. If you often reheat plates, sensor cooking earns its cost. Keep the cavity dry and wipe away fog, because a steamy interior skews sensor readings. Stir and rest food regardless of the mode, since no sensor can see a cold center.

The Sharp SMD2420MS pulls out like a drawer, so dishes slide in at waist height. A door unit like the Frigidaire swings open and needs the food lifted. Drawers cost more and need rails, but they suit accessible kitchens. Doors are cheaper and simpler to replace. A drawer also keeps the dish level as it slides, which matters when carrying soup. Plan the cabinet so the drawer clears nearby handles when fully open.

Frigidaire and Sharp have wider service networks than a lesser-known brand like AAOBOSI. A built-in is hard to swap, so repair access matters. Check warranty terms and local service before you commit, especially for combination units with convection parts. Ask whether the maker stocks the control board and the door latch, since those are the parts that fail most often. A cheap unit that cannot be repaired becomes an expensive cabinet cut.

specDecoder.meaning: The cutout is the opening in the cabinet or wall where the unit sits. It must match the body and trim kit.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Frigidaire PMBS3080BF lists about 24 3/4 in wide and 20 in deep, while the Summit is smaller.

specDecoder.meaning: A trim kit is the frame that fills the gap between the microwave and the cutout. It gives the flush look.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Frigidaire models sell kits separately, and the Summit includes one.

specDecoder.meaning: A sensor reads moisture to set power and time. It replaces manual timing for common foods.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Frigidaire Gallery, PMBS3080BF, FMBS2227BB and Sharp drawer have it.

specDecoder.meaning: Heat exits through the front rather than the back or top. It lets you install near walls or over a wall oven.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Summit lists it, so check others before placing them against a wall.

specDecoder.meaning: A fan circulates hot air around food for browning. It adds oven-like results to a microwave.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the AAOBOSI combo lists it among these picks.

howWeEvaluated.title: Install fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared body size, cutout and trim kit options from the spec sheets. The Summit's 22.5 inch opening is the smallest, and the Frigidaire PMBS3080BF lists the largest. Fit was weighted above features.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: Our comparison covered cubic feet across the lineup. The Gallery and PMBS3080BF reach 2.2 cu ft, while the Sharp drawer is 1.2 cu ft. Capacity was weighed against cabinet depth.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cooking aids
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted sensor cook, sensor reheat and convection modes. The Frigidaire models carry sensors, and the AAOBOSI adds convection. Aids that remove guesswork scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Accessibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered door versus drawer designs. The Sharp drawer opens at waist height, while door models need lifting. Accessible kitchens weighted this heavily.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership signals
howWeEvaluated.description: Long-term owner notes lean toward touch pads, door latches and magnetrons as wear points. A built-in is hard to replace, so service networks and trim kit availability earned credit.

cards.label: Door
cards.text: The Frigidaire models swing open and need food lifted over the lip. They cost less, and replacement is simple. They suit standard kitchens.

cards.label: Drawer
cards.text: The Sharp SMD2420MS pulls out at waist height with a 17 by 16 inch interior. It suits accessible kitchens and islands. It costs more and needs careful planning.

howToChoose.note: Pick the drawer for accessibility. Pick a door model for cost and simplicity.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A remodel needs a measured cutout, the right trim kit, a vent path and an outlet inside the cabinet. Confirm all four before ordering.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Frigidaire Gallery suits a large cabinet, the FMBS2227BB a standard opening, and the Summit a compact one. The Sharp drawer suits an island.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You need a very large cavity or accessible loading. The Gallery and Sharp drawer earn their cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You have a standard opening and basic needs. The FMBS2227BB or Summit give the built-in look for less.

maintenance.why: Baked-on splatter absorbs energy and can cause hot spots. Wipe while warm.
Covered vents let heat build up in a recessed cabinet. Vacuum dust from the slots.
A film of food residue stops the door from closing fully. Use mild soap and a soft cloth.
Spills on the Sharp drawer rails can stick the slide. Wipe them with a damp cloth.
Loose trim leaves gaps that collect crumbs. Tighten fasteners per the manual.

faq.q: What is the difference between a built-in and an over-the-range microwave?
faq.a: A built-in sits in a cabinet or wall cutout and usually needs a trim kit. An over-the-range unit mounts above the cooktop and includes a vent hood. Pick by the space you have.

faq.q: Do I need a trim kit?
faq.a: Most Frigidaire built-ins need one, sold separately in 27 inch and 30 inch sizes. The Summit SMBI24 includes its kit. Check the listing for what is in the box.

faq.q: Can I replace a built-in with a countertop microwave?
faq.a: Yes, but you lose the flush look and counter space. A countertop unit such as the Panasonic in the same size class can fit the shelf. Consider a trim kit for a clean finish.

faq.q: Are microwave drawers worth the extra cost?
faq.a: They suit accessible kitchens and islands because dishes slide in at waist height. The Sharp SMD2420MS is an example. For standard kitchens, a door unit costs less.

faq.q: Is sensor cooking worth it in a built-in?
faq.a: It helps with varied reheats because the oven judges time. Frigidaire's three built-ins list it. Skip it if you mostly cook by time.

faq.q: How long do built-in microwaves last?
faq.a: Owners can plan on several years, with touch pads, latches and magnetrons as common failures. A built-in is harder to replace, so buy from a brand with good service reach.
